title: How to Run Isolated Tenant Kubernetes Clusters on Shared GPU Infrastructure | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: A hands-on tutorial from NVIDIA and vCluster showing three ML teams sharing a single NVIDIA L40S GPU, each with a fully isolated Kubernetes control plane (vCluster) and a hierarchical quota queue (KAI Scheduler, the open-sourced Run:ai technology) guaranteeing 0.33 GPU with burst to the full card. The closing thesis is explicitly anti-consumption: 'The answer isn't always more GPUs, but better utilization of infrastructure' — notable coming from the company that sells the GPUs.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's own developer blog closes by arguing organizations should improve GPU utilization rather than buy more GPUs, an explicitly anti-consumption message from the vendor whose revenue depends on GPU sales.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Vendor-led utilization tooling means enterprise GPU demand growth is partly offset by software-driven efficiency gains — a quiet drag on unit volumes that models based on workload growth alone will miss.
insights.quote: The answer isn’t always more GPUs, but better utilization of infrastructure.
insights.locator: Get started running isolated tenant Kubernetes clusters

insights.claim: The demonstrated configuration runs three separate ML teams' production-shaped workloads concurrently on one NVIDIA L40S with 48 GB VRAM, packing what would conventionally be three dedicated allocations onto a single card.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: A 3:1 consolidation ratio on inference-class workloads is a real capex lever for enterprises told they must buy per-team GPUs.
insights.quote: Together, KAI Scheduler and vCluster provide a dedicated cluster experience for three teams with zero waste on a single GPU.
insights.locator: Get started running isolated tenant Kubernetes clusters

insights.claim: The organizational failure mode described is that teams request their own clusters purely to regain autonomy, meaning GPU fragmentation is driven by governance friction rather than by technical capacity needs.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: If political isolation demands are what strand GPU capacity, the fix is software governance, not more hardware — reframing where AI infrastructure budget should go.
insights.quote: At a certain scale, teams might start asking for their own clusters just to regain autonomy.
insights.locator: Running a dedicated Kubernetes cluster per team

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler is presented as an open source, topology-aware Kubernetes scheduler purpose-built for GPU allocation, designed for clusters spanning thousands of nodes and high workload throughput.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: NVIDIA open-sourcing the acquired Run:ai scheduling stack commoditizes a layer that GPU-orchestration startups were monetizing, squeezing independent AI-infrastructure software vendors.
insights.locator: KAI Scheduler is a robust, efficient, and scalable

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler coexists with the default kube-scheduler rather than replacing it, with routing controlled per-pod by the schedulerName field — a low-commitment adoption path for existing Kubernetes estates.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Side-by-side installation removes the biggest barrier to scheduler adoption; expect faster enterprise penetration than rip-and-replace alternatives.
insights.quote: Any pod with schedulerName: kai-scheduler is handled by KAI Scheduler. Everything else goes through the usual kube-scheduler process.
insights.locator: KAI Scheduler is a robust, efficient, and scalable

insights.claim: The full feature set attributed to KAI Scheduler is GPU sharing with DRA Driver support, hierarchical queues with guaranteed quotas plus over-quota bursting, gang scheduling, and topology awareness.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Gang scheduling plus topology awareness are the specific features distributed training requires; their presence in a free tool undercuts paid schedulers' differentiation.
insights.locator: KAI Scheduler decides fairly who gets GPU slices

insights.claim: The Queue CRD models an org-to-team hierarchy where quota is the guaranteed minimum, limit is the maximum allowed, and overQuotaWeight controls how surplus capacity is divided — a three-parameter model for GPU budgeting.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for internal GPU chargeback: guarantee floors, cap ceilings, and weight the idle-capacity scramble.
insights.quote: Here, quota is the guaranteed minimum, limit is the maximum allowed, and overQuotaWeight controls how surplus is split.

insights.claim: In the demo each child queue is guaranteed 0.33 GPU with a limit of 1, so any team can burst to the entire physical GPU when the other two are idle — capturing utilization that static partitioning would strand.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Burst-above-quota is where the real utilization gain comes from; static MIG-style carving cannot reclaim idle time this way.
insights.quote: Each is guaranteed 0.33 of the GPU and allowed to increase to the full GPU when others are idle.

themes.theme: Control-plane virtualization as the isolation layer

insights.claim: vCluster gives each tenant its own API server, CRDs, and RBAC that is indistinguishable from a dedicated Kubernetes cluster while the underlying nodes and hardware stay shared, decoupling the isolation boundary from the hardware boundary.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Separating perceived isolation from physical isolation is the enabling primitive for GPU-as-a-service and neocloud multi-tenancy business models.
insights.quote: Each tenant cluster gets its own API server, custom resource definitions (CRDs), and role-based access control (RBAC), indistinguishable from a dedicated Kubernetes cluster, while sharing the underlying nodes and hardware.

insights.claim: The virtualized control plane is described as invisible to tenants with no shared control plane nodes, no in-cluster agent pods, and no lateral path between environments.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: 'No lateral path' is the security claim that decides whether this is deployable for regulated or external tenants — the load-bearing assertion to validate.
insights.quote: no shared control plane nodes, no in-cluster agent pods, and no lateral path between environments

insights.claim: The tutorial uses the vCluster shared-nodes model and explicitly scopes it to trusted internal teams, directing untrusted tenants needing node-, network-, and storage-level separation to vCluster private nodes instead.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: The honest boundary: shared-node GPU multi-tenancy is an internal cost-efficiency play, not a foundation for selling isolated GPU capacity to third parties.
insights.quote: For untrusted tenants needing node-, network-, and storage-level separation, the same pattern extends to vCluster private nodes.
insights.locator: The vCluster shared-nodes model is used

insights.claim: The concrete tenant demands driving isolation are mundane and version-related: one team wants its own CRDs, one wants cluster-admin to debug scheduling, and one is pinned to a different Kubeflow version.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Dependency-version conflict, not security, is the real driver of cluster sprawl — meaning the addressable problem is far larger than the security-motivated multi-tenancy market.
insights.quote: The NLP Team wants to install their own CRDs. The Vision Team wants cluster-admin to debug scheduling. The Recommender Team is on a different Kubeflow version.
insights.locator: The example in this post uses three teams

insights.claim: KAI Scheduler explicitly does not enforce GPU memory isolation at the hardware level when GPU sharing is used — applications must voluntarily respect their allocation, for example by setting --gpu-memory-utilization in vLLM.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: Cooperative rather than enforced memory limits means one misconfigured tenant can OOM the others — a real operational risk that caps how far fractional GPU sharing spreads in production.
insights.quote: It does not enforce GPU memory isolation at the hardware level when GPU sharing is used.
insights.locator: Note that KAI Scheduler handles scheduling

insights.claim: Under fractional sharing the GPU time-slices between CUDA contexts from each pod at kernel boundaries, and hard memory isolation requires NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU hardware partitioning, which KAI Scheduler can also schedule.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: MIG remains the only hard-isolation path, and it is only on supported hardware — a concrete reason enterprises upgrade to MIG-capable SKUs rather than sharing older cards.
insights.quote: Under the hood, the GPU time-slices between CUDA contexts from each pod at kernel boundaries.
insights.locator: Under the hood, the GPU time-slices

insights.claim: The integration requires disabling vCluster owner rewriting via setOwner: false, because KAI Scheduler's pod-grouper walks Kubernetes ownership chains to auto-group workloads and virtualization would otherwise hide the real hierarchy.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: A non-obvious required setting: gang scheduling silently breaks without it, which is the kind of integration fragility that slows enterprise adoption of stitched-together open source stacks.
insights.quote: The KAI Scheduler pod-grouper walks ownership chains (Job → Pod, Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod) to auto-group workloads.
insights.locator: Step 6: Spin up a vCluster per team

insights.claim: Everything from the KAI Scheduler install onward is portable to any Kubernetes distribution running the NVIDIA GPU Operator with Container Device Interface enabled, making GPU Operator plus CDI the actual dependency floor rather than a specific cloud.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: The GPU Operator is the chokepoint layer every GPU Kubernetes deployment passes through — NVIDIA controls it, and it is where platform lock-in actually sits.
insights.quote: Step 3 (KAI Scheduler) onward is identical on any Kubernetes that has the NVIDIA GPU Operator running with Container Device Interface (CDI) enabled.

insights.claim: The demo environment runs on an NVIDIA Brev GPU instance hosted on Nebius, with NVIDIA using a third-party neocloud rather than its own or a hyperscaler's infrastructure for its reference tutorial.
insights.speaker: Ekin Karabulut
insights.so_what: NVIDIA showcasing Brev on Nebius is a soft distribution endorsement for the neocloud tier it has invested in, worth tracking as a channel signal.
insights.quote: This demo runs on an NVIDIA Brev GPU instance on Nebius
